title: PostgreSQL Extensions and the "Anarchy in the Database" VLDB paper
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
I've noticed that people in the PostgreSQL community often glorify extensions as if they were part of the core PostgreSQL system, while criticizing forks as if they were entirely separate software. Both forks and extensions can make minimal changes to the PostgreSQL code or significantly alter its internals. Both can modify how data is accessed, with the same privileges as a superuser. For example, the fork or extension code can view data unencrypted and change it, bypassing any audit logs or controls, and access the OS as the postgres user. The primary technical difference lies in how they are deployed: forks modify the source code before compilation, whereas extensions modify the already compiled code using dynamic libraries. There is also a difference in perception: extensions are viewed as friends of PostgreSQL, while forks are seen as competitors.

Before diving deeper into extensions, I would like to clarify one thing. If you compile PostgreSQL from source yourself—even if you don't change a single line of code—I consider it a fork. There's no secure way to ensure no modifications were made (unlike compiled binaries with checksums), and the compiler itself might introduce different behavior on some systems. Your security team should consider it as a new software, even if you know that you compiled it from the official source.

PostgreSQL extensions can be compiled or installed from pre-packaged binaries, but they are not controlled plugins running within a subsystem. Instead, they replace functions like you can do by patching the binaries or hacking with LD_PRELOAD. You can think of them as patches. If you're familiar with databases that utilize patch sets for new features and one-off patches for bug fixes, you'll understand the problem. Patches must be merged to work correctly and need comprehensive testing, since you're operating on software distinct from all others. When discussing with senior developers, I compare it to the Windows DDL that we copied into the System32 folder, which faced numerous incompatibilities. But for a database senior DBA, there's another analogy in a VLDB paper, Anarchy in the Database: A Survey and Evaluation of Database Management System Extensibility:

To our knowledge, the first extensible DBMS was INGRES in the 1970s, with its support for UDFs written in C

I didn't work with INGRES but with Oracle Database, which implemented many similar features to compete with INGRES. "User exits" were written in C, compiled, and linked directly with the database server. Later, this approach was replaced with external procedures, enabling them to run in a separate process called the listener, which communicates through the network or RPC for better isolation.

I recommend reading Anarchy in the Database: A Survey and Evaluation of Database Management System Extensibility, which compares the extensibility of PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, Redis, and DuckDB. In this article, I summarize the problems you may encounter with PostgreSQL extensions. I admire PostgreSQL's extensibility, which has played a key role in its popularity, as it opened an extensive ecosystem.

I aim to summarize the problems raised by the VLDB paper without sounding critical. Using extensions with PostgreSQL is perfectly acceptable, but it's essential to understand the implications. Saying "Just use PostgreSQL" becomes more complicated when it involves "Just use PostgreSQL with Extensions". You need to determine which extensions are safe to use together and how they affect deployment and upgrade complexity. Alternatively, you can choose a managed service to simplify deployment. However, in that case, your cloud provider will determine which extensions are permitted on their platform, and you reduce the freedom you got with PostgreSQL. My experience may also bias me. I have played extensively with PostgreSQL extensions in non-production environments. For production, I’ve mainly dealt with databases that include features and extensions such as forks of PostgreSQL (e.g., AWS RDS, Aurora, YugabyteDB) or databases where all features are built-in (like Oracle Database in my past and MongoDB currently).

Here's my summary of the VLDB paper (I recommend reading it), illustrated with some examples I encountered.

Key Problems with PostgreSQL Extensions

1. Lack of Isolation and Safety Mechanisms

  • No enforced isolation: PostgreSQL provides extensions with a highly permissive, low-level API through the database's C code, granting them extensive access to the database's internals. In this study, PostgreSQL is the only one with no isolation or security. Note that AWS tries to address this with pg_tle
  • Extensions can interfere with each other: Multiple extensions can assign or replace the same hooks (function pointers), and their load order may alter behavior, resulting in unpredictable and non-deterministic outcomes, such as one extension overwriting another’s hook.
  • No sandboxing: Extensions written in C execute in-process without sandboxing, allowing a faulty or malicious extension to crash the server, corrupt data, or compromise security. It is essential to verify that the extension has the same quality as PostgreSQL. For example, pg_stat_statements can be trusted as it is part of PostgreSQL (contrib), and widely used.

2. Compatibility & Interoperability Issues

  • Extension incompatibility: The study discovered that approximately 17% of tested PostgreSQL extension pairs were incompatible, potentially leading to errors, server crashes, or inaccurate outcomes when used together.
  • No built-in system for extension interoperability: Extensions cannot be reliably depended upon, referenced, or coordinated with each other.
  • Hook chaining is fragile. The convention is for extensions to chain hooks, meaning they should call both their functions and any previously set ones. However, PostgreSQL does not enforce or verify this, so failures frequently occur when hooks are overwritten or not appropriately chained.

3. API and Versioning Pain

  • Internal APIs are unstable: Many extension APIs are essentially internal C functions and structures, not stable or versioned interfaces. As a result, breaking changes between PostgreSQL versions compel extension authors to rely on preprocessor macros and complex, version-specific code. Be sure that the extension that depends on specific versions of PostgreSQL will continue to be maintained. Devrim Gündüz, who maintains the PostgreSQL community packages, exposed this at pgconf.de in The world of PostgreSQL extensions
  • Frequent code duplication: Extensions frequently duplicate and alter significant portions of PostgreSQL’s source code, with approximately 16% of extensions including copied PostgreSQL code, because they require access to functions that are either not properly exposed or are marked static. For example, pg_hint_plan uses a hook for the whole query planner and must fork all the related code.

4. Security Risks

  • Privileges and security boundaries are weak: Extensions can bypass PostgreSQL’s permission system, which could result in privilege escalation or data exposure if the extension is faulty or malicious. Even a simple hook, such as check_password_hook, which is made available by pg_tle because it doesn't access the system, discloses the user's password to the extension code.
  • Cloud providers restrict extensions: Because of these risks, cloud providers like AWS RDS strictly limit which extensions can be installed and often modify them to eliminate harmful features. Managed services rarely allow access to the OS, and languages like PL/Python do pass the security requirements.

5. Poor Developer/Operational Experience

  • Reliance on manual hook logic: Complex or large-scale hooks, such as planner hooks, are powerful tools but can be challenging to use correctly, which may lead to compatibility and maintenance issues. There is an unofficial documentation of hooks: psql-hooks
  • Lack of an official extension ecosystem: Without an official package manager or repository such as Python’s PyPI or Rust’s Cargo, users find it challenging to track and manage extension quality, updates, and compatibility. A good attempt by Tembo was Trunk on https://pgt.dev/. Keep in mind that many extensions are not maintained by the same community as PostgreSQL. If there's only one maintainer, are you certain that security issues will be patched in a timely manner?
  • Testing and maintenance burden: Many extensions require workarounds for compatibility, such as duplicating code and performing extensive version checks, which lead to fragile and difficult-to-maintain codebases. One of the authors in the paper, Marco Slot, did many tricks to make Citus be an extension rather than a fork, and exposed some of the problems in The trouble with extensions

This summary from the VLDB paper highlights potential issues. However, I don't want to end this article without mentioning that there are many positive stories about extensions. For instance, PostGIS, which adds spatial functions and indexes to PostgreSQL, has been highly popular, powering projects such as OpenStreetMap and numerous large-scale spatial applications. Furthermore, certain extensions are more trustworthy because they operate with lower privileges and typically deploy only SQL and PL/pgSQL, providing a more controlled API. PostgreSQL is a complex ecosystem that allows extensive capabilities when you know how to select, combine, and operate the right tools. The simplicity of deploying extensions and the popularity of PostgreSQL may mask this complexity, but keep in mind that you are deploying highly coupled components that you will need to manage and upgrade later.
